_source: National Crime Records Bureau, Crime in India 2024 (Volumes I to III), and the Office of the Registrar General of India, Census 2011 via data.gov.in
_caveats: Registered crime measures reporting as much as it measures crime. Whether an incident becomes a case depends on whether the person harmed goes to a police station and whether that station writes it down, and both vary enormously between states. A state with more registered cases may be a state where reporting works.
This page therefore ranks states on what happened to the cases they did register -- chargesheeting, conviction, how much is still pending -- rather than on how much crime they have.

Conviction rate here is convictions as a share of trials completed in the year, which is how NCRB defines it. It is not the share of reported cases that end in a conviction: most cases are still pending, and they are counted in the pendency figures instead.
Cases pending at the end of the year include cases carried over from previous years, so a state can charge-sheet everything it received and still show high pendency from an older backlog.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code on 1 July 2024. NCRB reports cases under the two codes together as IPC/BNS, so the general category here covers both.

In NCRB's table of police disposal of crime against senior citizens (Table 6A.4), the total of cases for investigation is smaller than the sum of its own parts in 13 states and union territories, by 140 cases nationally. The rest of that table, including pendency, is built on the printed total, so the printed total is used here.
